newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Richardson sees end of UN parking saga this week.
newsitem.headline: Richardson sees end of UN parking saga this week.

text.p: U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson said on Monday new plans to crack down on U.N. diplomats who refuse to pay parking tickets should be settled within a week after more talks with New York City officials.
Richardson said the State Department wanted to make sure each U.N. delegation, regardless of size, had two parking spaces allocated to it and that "police do not unfairly target diplomats."

"We made progress over the weekend," he said. "The mayor has made some constructive noises and we are close to an agreement," he added, referring to Mayor Rudolph Giuliani. "The mayor has tentatively accepted the plan but we want to make sure that the city side is enforcing the plan."

At issue are new parking regulations for the 185 foreign embassies, called missions, accredited to the United Nations. Giuliani wanted to remove special license plates of diplomats who routinely ignored parking tickets and other violations.

But after the U.N. legal counsel said parts of Giuliani's plan, at first endorsed by Richardson, violated international law, the State Department, which issues the plates, came up with an alternative. It would deny the foreign missions a plate the next time they applied for one, which usually happens annually. This would punish the mission but not necessarily the same diplomat who received the tickets.

"Temperatures have cooled down," Richardson said. "The mayor realises the United Nations is important to the city but at the same time every diplomat should pay attention to the law. That is going to be the new policy."

The battle over the parking rules, which originally were to take effect on April 1, has angered New York residents who see diplomats flout parking regulations and created a vitriolic debate among some U.N. missions that escalated into a public relations disaster for the world body.

A U.N. committee dealing with the issue had voted to take the matter to the 185-member General Assembly but called off this action after Richardson on Friday presented them with a new plan that had the agreement of U.N. lawyers.

Giuliani told reporters on Monday he believed the new plan was not strong enough and urged the State Department to accept the original plan. "We will put public pressure on them (diplomats) to do what any honourable citizen would do, which is to obey the laws of the country you're living in," he said.

"The United Nations has a moral burden and the State Department should challenge the United Nations on that moral burden, not only to do something for the quality of life of the city of New York but in my opinion they might have been able to do something for the quality of the United Nations."

Giuliani had suggested that the United Nations could leave town and the waterfront site could be reclaimed for city buildings. He also said he would reclaim 30 of the 111 new parking spaces for diplomats he set aside as part of the original April 1 agreement and threatened to take others away.

The city, which earns about $3.3 billion annually from the U.N. presence, also released a list of dozens of countries that owe money for parking tickets in the first three months of 1997, among them the Soviet Union, which was dissolved at the end of 1991.
Separately, Russia leads the list of owed parking tickets with $528,000. Its ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, has said the mission, across the street from a police precinct, has been unfairly targeted.
"We certainly believe this is a welcome development," Lavrov said of the new plan, adding that his diplomats were under obligation to follow the rules if they were fairly implemented.
City officials claim diplomats ignored 134,281 tickets last year, each costing a minimum of $55.
